title: Bouncing Cursor Clears the Array
statement:
You get an array nums of non-negative integers that contains at least one 0. You place a cursor on some index s with nums[s] = 0 and give it a direction, left or right. Then repeat while the cursor is inside the array:

  • If the value under the cursor is 0, take one step in the current direction.
  • Otherwise subtract 1 from that value, reverse the direction, and take one step in the new direction.

The process ends when the cursor steps outside the array. A start (an index together with a direction) is good if every value is 0 at the end. Return how many good starts there are. The same index with the two directions counts as two starts.

examples.why: From index 1 there are 3 units on the left and 3 on the right. The cursor alternates sides, so both directions empty both sides. From index 3 the sides hold 5 and 1, and the right side runs dry long before the left.
From index 2 the left holds 4 and the right 3. Starting toward the bigger side (left) works: that side gets the extra bounce. Starting right fails. Index 0 has 0 vs 7 and fails both ways.
Two zeros, but each splits the total 4 as 1 vs 3 or 3 vs 1. Counting zeros is not enough.

hints: Simulate a few starts by hand. Each time the cursor hits a positive value it turns around. What does that say about how it alternates between the two sides of the start?
Every unit removed causes one turn, so the cursor takes units from the left and right of the start in strict alternation, beginning with the side it faces.

Let L be the total to the left of the zero and R the total to the right. Both directions work when L = R. Exactly one works when they differ by 1. None works otherwise. A running prefix sum gives L and R for every zero.

explain.intuition:
Watch what happens around the start. The cursor walks through zeros until it reaches a positive value, removes one unit there and turns around. It then walks back across the start to the other side and removes one unit there. So it alternates: one unit from the side it first faces, one from the other, one from the first, and so on. It falls off the array when the side it is heading to has nothing left.

So the whole simulation reduces to two numbers: L, the sum to the left of the start, and R, the sum to the right. If L = R, alternation empties both sides whichever way you start: 2 good starts. If they differ by exactly 1, starting toward the bigger side works, because that side gets the extra turn: 1 good start. Any larger gap leaves units behind: 0.
steps: Compute total, the sum of the whole array.
Walk left to right keeping left, the sum of everything before the current index.
At each index with value 0, set right = total − left.
Add 2 if left = right, add 1 if |left − right| = 1.
pitfalls: Counting every zero as good. The two sides must be balanced to within 1.
Counting 2 when the sides differ by 1. Only the direction toward the bigger side works.
In a simulation, reusing the mutated array for the next start. Each start needs a fresh copy.

solutions.title: Simulate every start
solutions.idea: Copy the array for each zero and each direction, run the bouncing cursor until it leaves, and check that everything is 0.

solutions.title: Compare the sums on each side
solutions.idea: The cursor takes units from the two sides in strict alternation, so only the left and right totals matter. A running prefix sum gives both for every zero.

followups: Prove the alternation claim: why can the cursor never take two units from the same side in a row?
Return, for each good start, how many steps the cursor walks before it leaves. Can you get that without simulating?
